[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Weight Regularization (L1, L2, Elastic Net) in Deep Learning"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Weight regularization is a fundamental technique used in deep learning to prevent overfitting. When a neural network is too complex relative to the amount of training data, it tends to learn the noise in the training set rather than the underlying data distribution. Regularization introduces a penalty to the loss function based on the magnitude of the network weights, discouraging overly complex models."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding L2 Regularization (Ridge)"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"L2 regularization, also known as weight decay or Ridge regularization, adds a penalty proportional to the squared magnitude of the coefficients. The modified loss function becomes Loss = Loss_Original + lambda * sum(w^2), where w represents the weights and lambda controls the regularization strength."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Drives weights toward zero, but rarely sets them exactly to zero."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Encourages diffuse, small weights across all features."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Improves model generalization by smoothing the decision boundary."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding L1 Regularization (Lasso)"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"L1 regularization, known as Lasso regularization, adds a penalty proportional to the absolute value of the weights. The modified loss function is Loss = Loss_Original + lambda * sum(abs(w)). Unlike L2, L1 can drive weights completely to zero."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Performs automatic feature selection by zeroing out insignificant weights."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Creates sparse models with fewer active connections."},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding Elastic Net"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Elastic Net combines both L1 and L2 penalties. The penalty term is a weighted sum of the L1 and L2 norms: lambda_1 * sum(abs(w)) + lambda_2 * sum(w^2). This approach bridges the gap between Ridge and Lasso, retaining the feature selection properties of L1 while maintaining the grouping effect and stability of L2."},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"Implementation in TensorFlow and Keras"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"Applying weight regularization in Keras is straightforward. You can import regularizers from tensorflow.keras and pass them to the layer constructor."},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras.models import Sequential
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Dense
from tensorflow.keras.regularizers import l1, l2, l1_l2

# L2 Regularization
model_l2 = Sequential([
    Dense(64, activation=\'relu\', kernel_regularizer=l2(0.01), input_shape=(784,)),
    Dense(10, activation=\'softmax\')
])

# L1 Regularization
model_l1 = Sequential([
    Dense(64, activation=\'relu\', kernel_regularizer=l1(0.01), input_shape=(784,)),
    Dense(10, activation=\'softmax\')
])

# Elastic Net (L1 + L2)
model_elastic = Sequential([
    Dense(64, activation=\'relu\', kernel_regularizer=l1_l2(l1=0.01, l2=0.01), input_shape=(784,)),
    Dense(10, activation=\'softmax\')
])"},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"Choosing the right regularization technique depends on your dataset and architecture. L2 is a great default choice for general weight decay, L1 is useful when feature sparsity is desired, and Elastic Net provides a robust hybrid solution for complex datasets with correlated features."}]
